read.sections.0.heading.source: Remembering is a choice made in the present
read.sections.0.heading.back: Commemoration is a choice made by people in the present

read.sections.0.text.source:
A monument is made at a particular time to remember something. Its subject may belong to a much earlier period. So studying it involves two historical questions. What is being remembered? And why did later people choose to remember it in this form? The artist, the people who commissioned it, its place and its audience all shape that public account.

In the 1880s, the French town of Calais commissioned a monument from Auguste Rodin. It would commemorate, or publicly remember, citizens linked with the Hundred Years' War. Rodin drew on the medieval writer Jean Froissart's account of the siege of 1347. In that account, six leading citizens offered themselves to England's King Edward III in exchange for the town's protection. Rodin's sculpture shows them setting out, when their fate was uncertain. It is a nineteenth-century interpretation of a medieval story, not an eyewitness record.
read.sections.0.text.note: glossary commemoration = การรำลึก (the reading also uses รำลึกถึง as the verb). Edward III = พระเจ้าเอ็ดเวิร์ดที่ 3 แห่งอังกฤษ, plain royal style. Hundred Years' War = สงครามร้อยปี.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A monument is made at one time to commemorate something. The monument's subject may be from a much older era. So studying a monument involves two history questions. What is being commemorated? And why did a later generation choose to commemorate it in this form? The artist, the people who commissioned it, the place and the audience all shape that society's story.

In the 1880s, the French city of Calais commissioned a monument from Auguste Rodin. This monument was for commemoration, or public remembering, of citizens connected with the Hundred Years' War. Rodin used the account of Jean Froissart, a medieval writer, who told of the siege of the city in 1347. According to that account, six leading citizens gave themselves up to King Edward III of England in exchange for protecting the city. Rodin's sculpture shows the moment they set out, while they still do not know what their fate will be. This work is a 19th-century CE interpretation of a medieval story, not an eyewitness record.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A monument helps people remember. It may be about a much earlier time. So we ask two questions. What is remembered? And why did later people remember it this way? The artist, the people who paid, the place and the viewers all matter.

In the 1880s, the town of Calais in France asked Rodin for a monument. It would commemorate some of its people from a long war. To commemorate means to remember in public. Rodin used a story by Jean Froissart, a writer from the Middle Ages. In 1347, an army surrounded Calais. Six leading men offered themselves to England's king, Edward III. In return, he would keep the town safe. Rodin shows the men as they leave, not knowing what will happen. He made it more than 500 years later.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Monuments help people remember. A monument may tell a story from a much older era. So we ask two questions. What are we remembering? And why did a later generation remember this story in this way? The artist, the people who paid, the place and the audience all matter.

In the 1880s, the city of Calais in France asked Rodin to make a monument. This monument was for commemorating the city's people from a long war. Commemoration is remembering in front of everyone. The story Rodin used comes from Jean Froissart, a writer from the Middle Ages. In 1347 an army came and besieged Calais. Six important men gave themselves up to King Edward III, the king of England. It was an exchange so the king would not harm the city. Rodin's work shows the moment the six men are leaving, not knowing what will happen. This work was made more than 500 years after that event.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Six citizens stand side by side

read.sections.1.text.source:
The group has six figures, each with a different gesture and expression. Rodin placed them all on one level instead of raising one above the others. Plain clothes and vulnerable poses make the monument very different from a statue of a victorious ruler on horseback. Here, civic courage, the courage of a town's citizens, appears as people facing a hard choice together. Each one responds in his own way.

The town council had first planned a monument to Eustache de Saint-Pierre, the best-known citizen in the group. By including all six, Rodin shifted attention toward a shared action. This was a choice about public memory as well as composition. Deciding whom to show helped define the story the town would remember in public.

A separate figure, Jean d'Aire, helps us study those decisions. The National Gallery of Art's version shows a clothed man standing firmly and holding a large key. His posture and hands give the figure weight. A whole group and a single study offer different views of the same larger project. Their size and the way they are displayed also affect how an audience meets them.
read.sections.1.text.note: glossary civic = ของพลเมือง (Thai has no adjective for it; the term appears as ความกล้าหาญของพลเมือง). It is an awkward headword; a reviewer may prefer พลเมือง with a different definition. Check.
read.sections.1.text.back:
This group has six people, each with a different pose and expression. Rodin placed everyone at the same level instead of raising one person higher than the others. The plain clothes and vulnerable-looking poses make this monument very different from statues of victorious rulers on horseback. In this work, civic courage, the courage of people in a city, appears as a picture of people facing a hard choice together. Each one responds in his own way.

At first the city council planned a monument to Eustache de Saint-Pierre, the most famous citizen in the group. When Rodin put all six in, attention moved to shared action. This was as much a choice about society's memory as a choice about composition. Deciding whom to show helped set the story the city would commemorate in public.

Another separate statue, Jean d'Aire, helps us study those decisions. The National Gallery of Art in Washington's version shows a clothed man standing firmly and holding a large key. His stance and hands make the statue look solid. The whole group and the single study figure give different views of the same large work. Size and the way of displaying also affect how viewers meet the work.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
The monument has six men. Each one moves and looks in a different way. Rodin put them all on one level. They wear plain clothes. Their poses look weak, not proud. They are not like a king on a horse. It shows civic courage. Civic means about a town and its people. Here, courage means facing a hard choice together. But each man reacts in his own way.

At first, the town wanted a monument to one man, Eustache de Saint-Pierre. He was the best known of the six. Rodin showed all six instead. So the monument is about a shared act. Choosing whom to show shaped the story the town remembers.

Rodin also made a single figure, Jean d'Aire. A man stands firmly and holds a large key. His body and hands look strong. Their size and how they are shown change how we see them.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
This monument has six men. Each moves and looks differently. Rodin placed everyone at the same level. They wear plain clothes. Their poses look weak, not proud. They are not like a king on horseback. This work shows civic courage. Civic means about a city and the people in the city. Courage here means facing a hard choice together. But each man reacts in his own way.

At first the city wanted a monument of one man, Eustache de Saint-Pierre. He was the most famous of the six. But Rodin showed all six. So the monument is about doing something together. The choice of whom to show shapes the story the city remembers.

Rodin also made a single statue called Jean d'Aire. This man stands firmly and holds a big key. His body and hands look strong. Size and the way of displaying change how we look at the work.

read.sections.2.heading.source: An artist's travels and a bronze's dates
read.sections.2.heading.back: The artist's travels and the bronzes' dates

read.sections.2.text.source:
Rodin's career also crossed borders. He grew up in a working-class district of Paris and trained in the decorative arts. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 disrupted work, he continued his career in Belgium. A later journey to Italy deepened his interest in Michelangelo's sculpture. Calling Rodin a French artist names an important connection. But his skills developed through particular schools, jobs and travel. Artistic culture was shaped by movement as well as by local institutions.

Dates need particular care with sculpture. A model can be made first, and a bronze cast, an object formed in a mould, can be produced much later. The Met's group was modelled in 1884–95 but cast in 1985. The National Gallery of Art's smaller Jean d'Aire was modelled in 1884–89 and probably cast in 1895. Neither is a bronze made at the time of the medieval event, and each museum object is a separate cast.
read.sections.2.text.note: glossary cast = งานหล่อ; bronze = สำริด; mould = แม่พิมพ์; working-class = ชนชั้นแรงงาน; decorative arts = ศิลปะการตกแต่ง; Franco-Prussian War = สงครามฝรั่งเศส-ปรัสเซีย.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Rodin's working life also crossed borders. He grew up in a working-class neighbourhood of Paris and trained in decorative arts. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 interrupted work, he went to keep working in Belgium. A later trip to Italy made him more interested in Michelangelo's sculpture. Calling Rodin a French artist names one important connection, but his skills developed through particular schools, jobs and travels. Artistic cultures are shaped by moving from place to place as much as by local institutions.

For sculpture, you must take special care with dates. A model may be made first, and then a bronze cast, an object formed in a mould, may be made much later. The Metropolitan Museum of Art's group was modelled in 1884–95 but cast in 1985. The National Gallery of Art in Washington's small Jean d'Aire was modelled in 1884–89 and probably cast in 1895. None is a bronze made at the time of the medieval events, and each object in a museum is a separate cast.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Rodin's life also crossed borders. He grew up in a part of Paris where working people lived. He learned to make decorations. A war in 1870 and 1871 stopped much of the work, so he worked in Belgium. Later, in Italy, he studied Michelangelo's sculpture. Rodin was French. But his skills came from schools, jobs and travel.

Dates need care with sculpture. First an artist makes a model. Then a bronze cast is made, maybe much later. A cast is made by pouring metal into a mould. The Met's group is from a model made in 1884–95. But it was cast in 1985. The smaller Jean d'Aire is from a model made in 1884–89. It was probably cast in 1895. Neither was made in 1347. Each one is a separate cast.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Rodin's life also crossed borders. He grew up in a part of Paris where manual workers lived. He learned to make decorations. War in 1870 and 1871 stopped a lot of work, so he went to work in Belgium. Later, in Italy, he studied Michelangelo's sculpture. Rodin was French, but his skills came from schools, work and travel.

For sculpture, you must be careful with dates. First the artist makes a model. Then a bronze cast is made, which may be much later. A cast is made by pouring metal into a mould. The model of the group in New York was made in 1884–95, but the cast was actually made in 1985. The small statue called Jean d'Aire has a model from 1884–89, and the cast was probably made later, in 1895. None was made in 1347, when the event happened. Each one is a separate cast.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The siege story turns on six citizens offering their lives to save their town, during a war. Keep the account brief and non-graphic, and don't ask for any reenactment or role-play of the threatened people. The Franco-Prussian War is named only as the reason Rodin moved to Belgium for work.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: The siege story centres on six citizens offering their lives to save their city in wartime. Tell it briefly without violent detail. Do not have learners role-play or act out scenes of people under threat. The Franco-Prussian War is mentioned only as the reason Rodin moved to work in Belgium.

educatorNotes.0.source: An old-looking monument is not necessarily from the time of the event it shows. Keep three dates apart: the siege (1347), the model (1884–95, or 1884–89 for Jean d'Aire) and each bronze's casting date (1985 for The Met's group, probably 1895 for the National Gallery of Art's figure).
educatorNotes.0.back: A monument that looks old does not necessarily come from the era of the event it shows. Separate three kinds of date: the year of the siege (1347), the years the model was made (1884–95, or 1884–89 for Jean d'Aire) and the year each bronze was cast (1985 for the Metropolitan Museum of Art's group, and probably 1895 for the National Gallery of Art, Washington's statue).

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a group of citizens on one level, varied gestures, vulnerability alongside courage; a town commission in the nineteenth century commemorating a much earlier event, and the council's first plan for Eustache de Saint-Pierre alone. Accept other supported readings; don't require a single definition of heroism.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: a group of citizens on the same level, varied poses, vulnerability alongside courage, a 19th-century CE city commission to commemorate a much older event, and the city council's first plan for Eustache de Saint-Pierre alone. Accept other interpretations supported by evidence; do not require a single definition of heroism.

educatorNotes.2.source: The Froissart-based story, the group composition and the commission come from The Met's educator resource on The Burghers of Calais (PDF, printed pages 11–12 and 16). Its chronology separates the council's decision in 1884 from Rodin's selection in 1885; the reading says "in the 1880s". The Hirshhorn's account confirms the civic commission; its photographs are not open for reuse.
educatorNotes.2.back: The Froissart-based story, the group's composition and the commission come from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's resource for educators on The Burghers of Calais (PDF printed pages 11–12 and 16). Its timeline separates the city council's decision in 1884 from the choice of Rodin in 1885; the reading uses “in the 1880s”. The Hirshhorn Museum's description confirms the city's commission, but that museum's photographs are not open for reuse.

educatorNotes.3.source: Rodin's background (Paris, decorative-arts training, work in Belgium, Italy) comes from Clare Vincent's essay for The Met, Auguste Rodin (1840–1917). The essay shows adult-themed works elsewhere, so use only that background passage and don't send learners to it unfiltered.
educatorNotes.3.back: Rodin's background (Paris, training in decorative arts, work in Belgium, and Italy) comes from the essay Auguste Rodin (1840–1917) written by Clare Vincent for the Metropolitan Museum of Art. That essay has works with adult content elsewhere, so use only the background part, and do not send learners to read that essay without screening it.

educatorNotes.4.source: The National Gallery of Art's Jean d'Aire is a reduction (a smaller version) cast probably in 1895, not part of The Met's group or a full-size figure. The Met's group was cast in 1985 by the Coubertin Foundry; keep the cast date in its caption.
educatorNotes.4.back: The National Gallery of Art, Washington's Jean d'Aire is a reduced-size (smaller) version, probably cast in 1895; it is not part of the Metropolitan Museum of Art's group and not a life-size statue. The Metropolitan Museum of Art's group was cast in 1985 by the Coubertin foundry. Keep the cast date in the caption.
